sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Angers is redesigning its centre around walking and cycling while keeping street parking priced in two zones. As shown on the metropolis pages, the orange zone charges 1.70 euros for one hour, 3.40 for two and 6.60 for three, with a four-hour maximum, and the green zone 0.80 euro for one hour and 6.40 euros for eight, with a nine-hour maximum; not paying or underpaying costs 27 euros [4]. Residents of paid zones can get a status that allows free on-street parking in the evenings and nights, and an unlimited resident pass costs 55 euros a month or 500 a year in the orange zone and 15 a month or 100 a year in the green zone [5]. The metropolis says the hyper-centre has more than 9,500 paid parking spaces, with six free park-and-ride sites near the tram [16].

On 29 June 2026 the city council started an urban study on laying out and calming the centre; the article gives no timetable and no parking measures [3]. From 1 September 2026 a municipal order was announced to bar electric scooters and other motorised devices from the pedestrian plateau, with a 150-euro fine [2]. The Loire Angers development council, an advisory body, wrote in September 2025 that several park-and-ride sites are saturated and recommended reducing parking for non-residents [1]. A trade federation article of January 2025 said that unclassified vehicles were barred from the low-emission zone in the centre, but its current status was not checked [0]. The Irigo network recorded 44 million trips in 2025, one million more than in 2024 [13].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text: The main event is the new Parking du Château. The operator announced on 23 April 2026 that it would open on 27 April with 300 car spaces and 100 bike spaces, to compensate for on-street spaces removed in the redesign of the Kennedy and Académie squares, and that it is reversible so it can later be converted into offices or housing [9]. A city presentation of September 2024 had forecast 230 entries a day in 2027, rising to 520 in 2040, against 1,700 to 2,200 a day at Ralliement and 200 to 400 at Molière [11]. The page for the car park listed 14 electric-vehicle bays, not yet in service on 21 October 2026 [8]. It follows a 2022 decision in principle to entrust the Académie car park to Alter Services under a 25-year contract, with the final contract to be approved later and opening then expected in the second half of 2025 [10]. The Ralliement car park reopened fully on 26 September 2026 after works since May [12].

sections.title: Operators, positioning and utilisation
sections.text:
Alter Services, a local public company owned 55.3% by the metropolis and 44.7% by the city, runs paid on-street parking and the metropolis's multistorey and enclosed car parks [14]. In 2017 it ran 16 car parks under seven delegation contracts, with nearly 3,000 monthly subscribers and revenue of 5.86 million euros, 77.5% of it hourly [17]. At Ralliement the first hour is free and further hours cost 2.80 euros, with a night rate of 3 euros [6]; at Saint-Laud 2 the first 30 minutes are free and an hour costs 2.50 euros [7]. A real-time feed for 18 car parks is published on data.gouv.fr [15].

Our data cover those 18 car parks, 5,158 spaces, measured since 5 October 2026, and they are among the fullest we have seen. Occupancy averaged about 68% on weekdays and 53% at weekends, weighted by spaces. Saint-Laud (450 spaces) averaged 91% and was close to the same at weekends, Saint-Laud 2 (576) 87%, Molière (416) 79% and Le Mail (960) 72% on weekdays, falling to 48% at weekends. Most of the larger car parks reached or came close to full in single readings. Ralliement, the one the city says draws 1,700 to 2,200 entries a day, averaged 65%. The quietest are Le Quai (180) at 28%, Maternité (56) at 30% and Larrey (28) at 36%. The new Château car park does not appear in the feed. These are two and a half weeks of data.
